title: Return Dispersion- The 2025 Story - Systematic Investor - Ep.380 [REUPLOAD]

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Return Dispersion- The 2025 Story - Systematic Investor - Ep.380 [REUPLOAD].docx

speakers: Jim Kasang (Kai Wealth, name as transcribed)
summary: Year-end 2025 panel on return dispersion among trend followers: market selection, speed and vol-sizing around Liberation Day, flows into non-correlated assets, manager evaluation and track-record length.

coverage.note: intro and agenda; Katie on 2025 dispersion from April shock
rebalancing delay; speed vs V-shapes; 25-year speed ranking
speed conclusion; client questions; classification; non-correlated assets growth
AUM growth figures and drivers; perceived vs true non-correlation
bull vs bear uncorrelated; reflexive flows; vol compression
fees; dispersion and growing the pie
objectives and metrics; dispersion unhealthy view
premium change vs crowding; fees; outro

completeness_estimate: 0.78 - first reader caught each speaker's main thesis and the statistics; missed several supporting mechanisms (three-day shock structure, study method, capacity and supply-demand thesis, Katie/Andrew on investor segments, hindsight, hypothesis choice, fee drift) and mislabelled one speaker (no speaker labels in the caption).

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: you've had some sizable return dispersion this year across different managers and this is definitely prec precipitated by this huge
claims.claim: 2025 saw sizable return dispersion between trend managers, triggered by the April Liberation Day shock.
claims.conditions: after large shock

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: If you select the 10 largest markets, that has performed significantly better than sort of a diversified approach this year.
claims.claim: In 2025 a 10-largest-markets universe beat a broadly diversified one (gold allocation drove it), so market-set choice created big dispersion.
claims.conditions: 2025, idiosyncratic

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: very slow trend strategies and very fast trend strategies weathered the storm this year
claims.claim: In 2025 very slow and very fast trend strategies did best around the April shock, while ~8-month windows did worst.
claims.conditions: V-shaped shock

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: volatility adjustment that was faster would be able to navigate and forget uh what happened in that giant 3-day shock
claims.claim: Faster volatility estimation handled the three-day Liberation Day shock better than stable vol sizing; in 2022 faster was also better.
claims.conditions: extreme multi-day vol shock

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: subtle decisions in your allocation, subtle decisions in speed created very very different results
claims.claim: In extreme years small choices in universe, speed and vol-sizing produce very different results; each year differs for price-based trend.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: imagine if you just trade gold and you know or oil or just and corn um you would see that those happen to be the markets that tra t trended the best this year idiosyncratically
claims.claim: Gold, oil and corn trended best in 2025 idiosyncratically, not over a 25-year history, so concentration helped this year only.
claims.conditions: 2025 only

correction.issue: Attributed to Andrew Beer, but the passage comes from a panelist before Niels says 'Yeah, Andrew, you raised ...'; Andrew speaks only afterwards (and about replication concentration). Speaker is unidentified in the captions.
correction.fix: Unidentified panelist (not Andrew Beer): a portfolio of just gold, oil and corn would have trended best in 2025 idiosyncratically, which is not true over a 25-year history, so market-selection gains in 2025 were specific to the year.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: there is somewhat of a delay in terms of our rebalancing definitely helped us around liberation day
claims.claim: Slow rebalancing helped around Liberation Day because shorter-term models and vol controls reacted to every Trump headline; concentration in two currency contracts hurt on euro and helped on yen.
claims.conditions: headline-driven reversals

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: the shorter term models actually weren't as bad which was interesting. It was more the mid-range
claims.claim: The mid-range trend speed (6-8 months) overreacted and did worst, shorter models less badly.

claims.speaker: Nick Balters
claims.quote: If you're too quick in a Vshape, you'll get some of the first part and some of the second part right. If you're too slow, you just stomach the first part.
claims.claim: In V-shaped markets fast signals capture both legs, slow signals only absorb the first leg and then recover fully, while intermediate speeds are caught both ways (soldiers on bridge).
claims.indicator: trend speed vs V-shapes (Aug 2024, SVB, Liberation Day)
claims.conditions: V-shaped reversals

claims.speaker: Nick Balters
claims.quote: The last three years at least based on our calculations have been the only three years in the last 25 that the longest speed or the slowest was always the best.
claims.claim: 2023-25 are the only three consecutive years in 25 where the slowest trend speed was best, and a small universe was first or second best; in 2022 the fastest was best.
claims.indicator: trend speed and universe size by year

claims.speaker: Nick Balters
claims.quote: year on year the longer you are or the longer time you are in your signals you would have done better which is the exact contrast to what we had in 2021 2022
claims.claim: Year on year slower signals did better in 2023-25 versus faster in 2021-22, while locally the middle speeds were worst.

claims.speaker: Yov Git
claims.quote: the models that actually performed the best are actually the ones that were slower
claims.claim: Clients asked whether to speed up in response to Trump uncertainty, but slower models performed best.

claims.speaker: Mark Resiminski
claims.quote: I call it a a three factor classification which called STM style timing in markets
claims.claim: Classify CTAs on three dimensions: style (e.g. vol response), timing (speed) and markets; build a portfolio of managers spread across them.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: there's a clear [L160] difference between what worked prior to 2022 and what's worked in the last 3 years
claims.claim: The Quantica paper concludes what worked before 2022 differs from the last three years, supporting dynamic parameter selection rather than static parameters.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: the massive correlated growth of non-correlated assets
claims.claim: Precious metals, crypto, structured products and hedge funds have all grown massively together, driven by demand for non-correlation.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: Fast forward three years, they've all doubled, tripled, quadrupled in assets.
claims.claim: Hedge funds went from about 2T to 4.5T, crypto 1.5T to 4.5T, precious metals 3T to 9T and structured products 0.5T to 2T over three years, against roughly 400-500T of long-only assets.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: there's only 20 trillion in uncorrel correlated assets relative to call it 4 to500 trillion on the other side
claims.claim: Only about 20T sits in uncorrelated assets versus 400-500T in long assets, so the flow into non-correlated strategies is early, and likely to rise if long assets underperform or rates rise.
claims.conditions: higher rates, weak long assets

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: the breakdown in correlation between stocks and bonds in uh in 22 is a huge driver of this
claims.claim: Drivers of demand for non-correlation: higher rates, 2022 stock-bond correlation break, record valuations, rising debt and loss of US hegemony.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: things that are perceived as non-correlated and which absolutely recently have empirically been non-correlated. That doesn't mean to say that they won't be non-correlated
claims.claim: Recent non-correlation of assets like crypto and gold may not hold in a market shock; only designed tail strategies are non-correlated by construction.
claims.conditions: market shock

claims.speaker: Yov Git
claims.quote: there are different type of investors who went into each of those markets
claims.claim: Different investor types drive each theme: retail into crypto, central banks into gold, allocators into hedge funds; the total-portfolio approach seeks assets uncorrelated to long-only beta.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the flipping correlation of stocks and bonds the fact that everything went down together the fact that bonds had a draw down that was 4x
claims.claim: After 2022 (bond drawdown 4x prior 20 years) every asset-allocation model must incorporate positive stock-bond correlation; gradual allocator education drives demand for futures-based ETFs.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: assets and strategies that are uncorrelated with equities in a bull market and those are uncorrelated with equities in a bare market
claims.claim: Distinguish strategies uncorrelated in bull markets (liquidity-driven, e.g. crypto, gold) from those uncorrelated in bear markets (convexity in stress, e.g. trend); credit is the classic false diversifier.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: the most scalable strategies tend to be the most simple um, and often uh, imperfect
claims.claim: Scalable strategies are simple and imperfect, and large flows into them have reflexive effects on the underlying assets.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: V compression that's natural uh flow overwhelms the amount of liquidity and other flows
claims.claim: In summers, structured-product issuance compresses index vol, which causes constituent dispersion and pain in crowded long-short equity.
claims.indicator: index vol compression, dispersion, long/short equity crowding
claims.conditions: low liquidity summers

claims.speaker: Nick Balters
claims.quote: we will experience correlations not in a back test but in reality
claims.claim: Allocators holding historically uncorrelated strategies for the same goal will all cut risk on a VIX shock, producing correlation in reality that a backtest misses.
claims.conditions: shocks

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: 6040 as a strategy really didn't exist until the 19 mid1 1980s
claims.claim: 60/40 only became standard in the mid-1980s; stock-bond correlation was positive for the 80 years before 1982, and non-correlated strategies also offer capital efficiency which draws flows as rates rise.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: it's a supply and demand story for certain strategies with certain managers of certain characteristics
claims.claim: Fees for scarce strategies (discretionary macro, multistrats) have risen in the past 1-2 years because of supply and demand.

claims.speaker: Nick Balters
claims.quote: this performance dispersion can also be a bit of a hurdle to grow further
claims.claim: Large dispersion between CTAs (+15 to -15) triggers aggressive selection and investment committee concerns that can slow industry growth.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: people invest in what they like
claims.claim: Investor preferences are heterogeneous; CTA outcomes feel random so luck is easily mistaken for skill.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: diversification is the one thing that if you can you know that that is free
claims.claim: When there is no strong edge in selecting managers, diversify allocation across them.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: if you look at a return series where you buy the top manager and and sell the bottom one
claims.claim: Switching between top and bottom managers produces much worse investor outcomes than holding the space, so dispersion worsens behavioural return-chasing.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: what made us comfortable in all of this was the robustness of it
claims.claim: Replication design choices (lookback, factors) matter little; robustness to switching them gives comfort.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: they do it with almost like a like an exaggerated sense of confidence like it was obvious
claims.claim: CTA managers present design choices with exaggerated confidence, inviting questions about why the change was not made earlier.

claims.speaker: Yov Git
claims.quote: the obviousness comes from uh what are we providing to investors which may be different to what everybody else is is providing
claims.claim: Design is clear when tied to the investor objective (liquid high-beta markets for macro factors, alternative markets for inflation/commodity factor, high-frequency for convexity).

claims.speaker: Yov Git
claims.quote: you don't really want alternative markets. It makes no sense to you.
claims.claim: Investors who just want long-term equity trend need not hold alternative-market CTAs.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: if we're relying on a a precedent regime I tend to think that's overfitting curve fitting
claims.claim: Design decisions are never obvious; relying on a precedent regime is overfitting, and Winton's decade of reducing trend followed by trend resumption shows behavioural drift.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: I actually think it's very healthy um in in our trend following sector
claims.claim: Dispersion across trend followers is healthy, but managers must explain their objectives since investors judge all by the same metrics.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: there are different metrics for different objectives
claims.claim: Different trend objectives (smooth outcome, outlier hunting, crisis alpha) need different metrics, and underperformance should be explained against the objective (no outliers in the period).

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: it's about making the decisions and design decisions based on that objective
claims.claim: Design decisions follow the program objective (CTA-like one-stop product vs risk mitigation vs convexity).

claims.speaker: Mark Resiminski
claims.quote: I think it actually is unhealthy in the sense is that then it's harder to classify what is a CTA
claims.claim: Dispersion is unhealthy since it blurs what a CTA is and burdens managers to explain.

claims.speaker: Mark Resiminski
claims.quote: you go through other hedge fund strategies there probably is less dispersion
claims.claim: Other hedge fund strategies show less dispersion, so factors can describe and replicate them; CTAs mix trend with other embedded strategies.

claims.speaker: Yov Git
claims.quote: Well, dispersion basically means diversification.
claims.claim: Dispersion across fast/slow, alternative markets and liquid futures CTAs gives different alpha sources that can be combined into a more holdable portfolio.

claims.speaker: Yov Git
claims.quote: having a homogeneous high correlation to sort of an index in some sense is is is a problem
claims.claim: A homogeneous, index-like CTA universe is a problem because investors cannot tell managers apart.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: I think that randomness is very very hard for most allocators
claims.claim: Allocators struggle with randomness in trend returns because CTAs lack the rebound narrative equity long-short managers can offer; explanation is technical and leaves them unconvinced.

claims.speaker: Nick Balters
claims.quote: it's just a matter of aligning your culture to avoid overfitting and address the blind spots and acknowledge the trade-offs
claims.claim: Some dispersion is good; managers should avoid overfitting, address blind spots and match design to client needs.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: the amount of data you need to evaluate a manager and get to get conviction that they're realized sharp is or true sharp is way longer than what most investors realize
claims.claim: Statistical confidence in a manager's true Sharpe ratio takes 10+ years of data, yet investors judge on 1-3 years and recency.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: the two things that kind of input into the equation as to how long you need are the the degree of outperformance
claims.claim: Years of data needed depends on the size of outperformance and the correlation to the benchmark: high correlation shortens the test, obscure CTAs need much longer.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: To be honest 5% is ridiculous. Like most most people would be happy if they were 75% confident
claims.claim: The 5% significance level is too strict for allocation; 75% confidence is acceptable, allowing shorter evaluation periods.

claims.speaker: Yov Git
claims.quote: by the time by the time you think you actually have a statistical point of point of view
claims.claim: Statistics lag regime change: alternative markets took 10 years to be loved and then 1-2 weak years to be called crowded.

claims.speaker: Yov Git
claims.quote: you kind of need to understand also how the manager would um you know would have proper control over trading, over data
claims.claim: Manager selection should rest on sound design, operational due diligence, execution, data, and crisis response (Winton's drift from core trend and return).

claims.speaker: Nick Balters
claims.quote: If there's a fundamental reason why we build a systematic strategy, we have to assess the reasons why the initial premise is not there yet.
claims.claim: Change or retire a systematic strategy only when its underlying premium has changed, not on statistics; costs are a separate issue.

claims.speaker: Nick Balters
claims.quote: crowding would make the strategy underperform not flat out because flattening out
claims.claim: Commodity pre-roll (congestion) premium flattened around 2018-19 because investors rolled in the back of the curve; this is premium disappearance, not crowding, which only underperforms.

claims.speaker: Nick Balters
claims.quote: selling volatility is not a profitable strategy it's actually quite impossible because that goes against the economic nature of how investors operate
claims.claim: The bar to drop a strategy is high: selling vol will not stop paying since investors keep buying insurance.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: one of the FM issues in in in CTAs is we've seen a drift from performance only from performance related uh pay to um you know flat management fee
claims.claim: Allocators differ on fee structure: some prefer flat low fees (ETF, QIS), others want performance-fee alignment and skin in the game.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: what you saw around liberation day was three days in a row of extensive shocks, not one and then a quiet period and then a reversal
claims.claim: Liberation Day was three consecutive days of extreme moves (by turbulence metrics), not one shock followed by calm and a reversal, which made it a hard signal for price-trend and vol-sizing models; managers whose vol estimate forgot the shock faster coped better.
claims.direction: faster vol estimation improves response to consecutive-day shocks
claims.conditions: Shock clusters of several days; opposite in 2022 when speed hurt.
claims.testable: yes - compare vol-estimate half-life with returns around the shock

claims.speaker: Nick Balters
claims.quote: We literally just ranked anywhere from like know two month to a 12 month halfife
claims.claim: Nick's year-by-year study ranks trend speeds from 2 to 12 month half-lives across three universe sizes (about 10 markets, a few mid-size, and 80+ markets) for each of 25 years, which is how he finds that the slowest speed and a small universe won in 2023-25.
claims.indicator: trend half-life (2-12 months) by universe size, 25-year calendar-year ranking
claims.conditions: Calendar-year ranking of speeds and universes; depends on the chosen universes.
claims.testable: yes - the ranking exercise is replicable

claims.speaker: Nick Balters
claims.quote: It happened however that still a smaller universe was was was a better one to
claims.claim: Even in 2022, when the fastest speed was best, a smaller concentrated universe still beat the larger ones, so the small-universe advantage held across 2022-25 while the best speed switched from fastest to slowest.
claims.conditions: 2022-25 only; the long-run record may differ (see Andrew and Katie on the 25-year view).

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: it's hard to find capacity for non-correlated assets
claims.claim: Capacity is the constraint: there is little room in genuinely non-correlated assets, so the key question is how infrastructure and liquidity will be built (and what else can be seen as non-correlated) to absorb the inflows.
claims.indicator: capacity of non-correlated assets and strategies
claims.conditions: Because early adopters are arriving faster than infrastructure.
claims.testable: partly - capacity is hard to measure

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: they now have a bucket now they've had to figure out how to fill it
claims.claim: Allocators have created an alternatives bucket after 2022 but now have to work out what to put in it, so demand for products that fill the bucket (futures-based ETFs, replication, trend) is limited by knowledge, not by desire.
claims.conditions: Education is gradual.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: that's why Goldman just paid 2 billion for Innovator
claims.claim: Buffered and defined-outcome ETFs are an early-stage growth area in a 13 trillion dollar ETF market, evidenced by Goldman paying about 2 billion dollars for Innovator.
claims.indicator: buffered ETF market, Goldman acquisition of Innovator
claims.conditions: Data point supporting the 'still early' view.
claims.testable: yes - the deal and AUM are public

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: imbalance between uh people needing non-correlation and the amount of non-correlation available um that is maybe the most important thing to understand in finance
claims.claim: Jim's core thesis: flows into precious metals, crypto, structured products and hedge funds are driven by a supply and demand imbalance between investors needing non-correlation and the amount of it available.
claims.direction: non-correlated assets and strategies attract flows
claims.conditions: Holds while long assets and bonds fail to offset equity risk.
claims.testable: partly - flow data can be compared with correlations

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I wonder if this will actually change the fee compression at some point that we've seen because there might uh you know more demand for the best uh strategies
claims.claim: Niels asks whether rising demand for non-correlation will end fee compression for the best strategies; Alan's answer is that supply and demand already lifts fees for scarce managers.
claims.indicator: manager fees vs demand for non-correlation
claims.conditions: Applies to managers in short supply.
claims.testable: yes - fee levels by strategy type over time

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: these things are actually going to be the primary driver at some point of the underlying assets themselves
claims.claim: If inflows into structured products and hedge funds keep growing, their positioning could become the primary driver of underlying asset behaviour, which could be a structural risk to correlations and liquidity in future years.
claims.indicator: structured product and hedge fund flow impact on markets
claims.conditions: Depends on continued growth of these flows (his thesis, not shown).
claims.testable: partly - flow impact on volatility and dispersion can be studied

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: when you have a 20% difference between one product and another
claims.claim: With about 20% spread between trend products in a year, every manager takes a turn at the bad end, so investor education about dispersion is needed for the industry to grow.
claims.conditions: Applies to investor adoption.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: most of the assets are really in the institutional space
claims.claim: Managed-futures assets sit mostly with institutions; ETFs and other wrappers are widening access to a different investor universe that has not held these strategies before.
claims.conditions: Katie cites her paper from last year.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: can recognize the statistical benefits of a 3 or 5% allocation to the strategy but does not want to spend a year getting up to up the learning curve
claims.claim: A product niche exists for model-portfolio allocators who see the statistical benefit of a 3-5% managed-futures sleeve but will not spend a year learning how to evaluate dispersion; a replication ETF serves them.
claims.conditions: Applies to model allocators without a manager-selection function.
claims.testable: no - description of a client segment

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: people who will view dispersion as a huge positive because it allows them to make you know allows them to pick somebody who did well last year
claims.claim: Some investors treat dispersion as an opportunity to pick last year's winner or drop laggards and reconfigure; others want a simple beta-like solution, so products must fit different preference functions.
claims.conditions: The first style risks return-chasing (see Katie's point on investor outcomes).

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: this space has has a a perception of a lot of randomness
claims.claim: In some hedge fund categories allocators believe in identifiable star managers, but trend following is seen as random, so luck and skill are hard to separate and the answer investors want is skill.
claims.conditions: The narrative problem is in separating luck from skill.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: managers who became very popular only to see their AUM implode uh in the following years
claims.claim: Niels recalls cases over the last decade or two of managers who became very popular and then lost most of their assets, a bad outcome for the underlying investor, which supports the argument that performance chasing hurts.
claims.conditions: Anecdotal; no names given.
claims.testable: yes - AUM flows vs subsequent returns

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: I inevitably find when people say that it's from a position of hindsight um so it's very easy from that position to actually say something's very obvious
claims.claim: Claims that a design decision was obvious come from hindsight; every design involves trade-offs and uncertainty, so the future should be treated as unknown rather than relying on the regime that just worked.
claims.conditions: Contrasts with Andrew's observation that managers present choices with confidence.

claims.speaker: Yov Git
claims.quote: holding a CTA is actually very difficult because you know it's a sharp one strategy maybe a little bit less maybe a little bit more um and it's kind of difficult to to sit within my IC
claims.claim: A CTA is hard to hold in an investment committee because a Sharpe-about-1 strategy has losing years and the committee asks why it lost money, so a mix of CTA types can make the allocation easier to hold.
claims.indicator: CTA Sharpe ratio, investment committee patience
claims.conditions: Applies to institutions with committee oversight.
claims.testable: partly - depends on the Sharpe and loss frequency

claims.speaker: Yov Git
claims.quote: it actually gives the investor a true choice and also clarity about when each of these component is likely to perform
claims.claim: If trend programs state different objectives and target distinct risk factors, investors can see when each component should perform, gain confidence, and hold each through its expected off-periods.
claims.indicator: trend program objectives and risk factors
claims.conditions: Requires managers to state objectives.
claims.testable: partly - behaviour and retention are hard to test

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: would have predicted the outcome that that Nick laid out in terms of very very long-term models work
claims.claim: No one four years ago would have predicted that very slow models on major markets would win for three years, which is why design winners are unforecastable, while allocators look for a manager who says 'I knew that would happen'.
claims.direction: slow models and small universe won 2023-25
claims.conditions: Hindsight: unforeseeable at the time.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: you've got other biases career risk very hard to defend you know an underperforming manager
claims.claim: Manager selection is distorted by after-the-fact narratives for whoever is doing well, recency bias and career risk (it is hard to defend an underperformer), so investors judge on short performance despite the long data needed.
claims.conditions: Applies to allocators and investment committees.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: Are we talking about what a statistician would call a test against a hypothesis of zero returns?
claims.claim: The data needed depends on the test: showing a manager's return is positive (zero hypothesis) needs less data than showing they beat a benchmark by a stated margin, so allocators should specify the hypothesis before asking how long.
claims.indicator: statistical test design for manager evaluation
claims.conditions: A 20% outperformer is found quickly; a 50bp outperformer takes much longer.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: the more dispersion is in the industry, the harder it is to say whether people are outperforming other people
claims.claim: Greater dispersion across the industry makes it harder to tell managers apart statistically because the differences look random, which links dispersion to longer evaluation periods.
claims.conditions: Lower correlation between managers means more data.
claims.testable: yes - from correlations and tracking error

claims.speaker: Yov Git
claims.quote: what aspects of your trading you can actually improve on. Is it execution? Is it risk management
claims.claim: After three difficult years investors ask how a manager responds to a drawdown while staying true to trend following; the acceptable answers are improvements to execution, data and risk management, not a drift away from the core approach.
claims.conditions: Winton is the example of drift away from the core and back.

claims.speaker: Nick Balters
claims.quote: maybe dispersion becomes a better theme but there is no particular reason to actually feel that tomorrow you know investors become risk loving
claims.claim: Large structured-product demand can shift where the volatility premium is best harvested (dispersion may become a better expression), but investors are not becoming risk-loving, so the premium for providing insurance remains.
claims.conditions: Depends on structured-product flows.
claims.testable: partly - dispersion vs index vol premia are observable

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: we've seen a drift from performance only from performance related uh pay to um you know flat management fee
claims.claim: CTA fee structures have drifted from performance-related pay toward flat management fees; some allocators prefer low flat fees (ETFs, QIS), while others want managers to take performance fees and have skin in the game.
claims.conditions: Allocator preference differs.
